title: Medical reversal and de-adoption meta-record: identifying contradicted practices is not the same as removing them from care
summary: Adds a meta-research audit record for medical reversal and de-adoption. The record links reversal-counting work to de-adoption literature, explicitly separating “a randomized trial contradicted a practice” from “the practice disappeared from real care.”

claims.claim: The de-adoption lane must separate medical reversal identification from actual de-adoption; knowing a practice is low-value is not equivalent to changing reimbursement, guidelines, clinician behavior, or patient expectations.
what_would_change_status: A future de-adoption theory better separates these stages.

claims.claim: This meta-research record is not a prevalence estimate for all medicine; it is a method surface showing that reversal-after-adoption is measurable and that de-adoption requires its own evidence infrastructure.
what_would_change_status: A broader systematic estimate for all clinical practice supersedes the scope statement.

evidence_profile.source_depth: one-pass source-backed extraction; child record and second-pass systematic-review extraction required for mature synthesis
limitations: Not medical advice and not a current clinical recommendation engine.
Uses exact indication/population/endpoints available in one-pass sources; child records needed for all subgroups and guideline dates.
Practice-lag claims require fuller utilization and reimbursement child records before maturity.

denominator_surface: journals and RCTs that test current practices
numerator_surface: current practices contradicted or found ineffective

handling_notes: Clinical reversals can involve real patients who made choices under uncertainty; avoid hindsight contempt.
Do not treat procedure de-adoption as a patient-specific treatment recommendation.
Preserve the difference between “no benefit in studied population” and “never useful.”
